description: API-shape experiment for widget-level editing: a multi-source sample audition board with source-time mapping and automation, and a piano roll with app-controlled editing plus a launcher scene grid. Expectations describe behaviour, not names.

tasks.prompt: A browser sample-audition board on `context`. In `row` it shows three players side by side with the toolkit's player widget: `wave` (a long loop that the page plays stretched to 0.8x speed, so a second of the source is not a second of output), `oneShot` (a decoded one-shot) and `streamed` (a streamed long file). (1) Give every player's waveform a dark theme: keep the toolkit's normal drawing and only tint it. (2) Clicking the `wave` waveform shows both numbers, the source second under the click and the output second under it, and seeks playback to that place. (3) While `wave` plays (not looping) its sound must dip to 0.3 between source seconds 4 and 6 through `gain` (the node the page routes it through), following the source seconds even though the output is stretched. (4) A new sample may start loading into `wave` while the old one is still loading; a Cancel button must stop the load so a late decode never shows up or sets an error. (5) Under the `wave` waveform draw a peak bar chart of its source audio at 256 frames per bar; clicking bar `n` shows its frame range and time range.
expectations: Mounts one player widget per source type using the toolkit's adapters for the wave player, the buffer player and the file player.
The custom waveform drawing reuses the toolkit's default drawing and only tints it.
The two numbers come from the player's own mapping between source and output seconds, and the seek goes to the output second of the click.
The dip is a source-time automation attached to the player (non-looping), driven by the player's playback and not by output seconds or a timer.
Cancel uses the player's own load cancellation so a superseded load publishes neither audio nor error.
The bars come from a peak summary of the source audio at 256 frames per peak and the click maps a bar to its frame range with the toolkit.

tasks.prompt: A browser editor with `clip`, a MIDI clip from the toolkit, shown in `host` with the toolkit's piano roll, and a scene launcher `launcher` shown in `gridHost`. (1) A double-click on an empty spot must not add a note by itself: the app gets the proposed note and decides, snapping it to a quarter of a beat, half a beat long, velocity 0.8, and adding it to the clip as one Undo-able edit of your own. (2) Deleting selected notes (keyboard) must ask the user (`confirm`) and then delete through your code. (3) A velocity lane shows under the roll. (4) The app has a list of notes next to the roll (`onNoteListClick(handler)` calls `handler(noteId)`); clicking one highlights that note in the roll without changing the roll's selection. (5) The clip plays only beats 4 to 12 of its content; the roll shows the rest dimmed and follows when that window changes. (6) Below, a grid of the launcher's scenes with one `Launch` button per scene: pressing a scene button must apply the launcher's own rule for tracks that are empty in that scene (the launcher stops those tracks), not just start the clips that exist.
expectations: The roll reports a proposed new note to the app instead of adding it, and the app adds a snapped note (quarter-beat snap, half a beat, velocity 0.8) through the clip's edit.
Deletion is reported to the app, which confirms and then deletes through the clip's edit.
The velocity lane is enabled on the roll.
The note list highlights the roll's active note through the roll's own handle, without changing its selection.
The playing window (beats 4 to 12) is given to the roll's model so the rest is dimmed, and follows changes.
Each scene row in the grid launches the scene by its slot index so the launcher's empty-slot rule applies.
